title: Numbers & time
description: Native and Sino-Korean numbers, counters, prices, clock time, days and dates.

items.note: Native 하나 둘 셋 count things and hours; before a counter 둘 becomes 두.
Before a counter 셋 becomes 세: 세 개, 세 명.
Counting aloud uses native numbers, e.g. before a photo.
Short form of 셋 used right before a counter: 세 잔, 세 시.
잔 counts cups with native numbers; 셋 shortens to 세 before it.

items.english: There are five people in my family.
items.note: People are counted with native numbers + 명: 한 명, 다섯 명.
distractors: There are four people in my family.
My family lives in five cities.

good.english: How many siblings do you have?

items.note: 마리 counts animals and fish, with native numbers: 한 마리, 두 마리.

distractors: My cat is two years old.

items.note: 권 counts books and volumes, with native numbers: 한 권, 세 권.

items.english: How many books did you buy?
distractors: Where did you buy the books?

bad.english: I bought them at a bookshop.

items.note: Native 20; right before a counter it becomes 스무: 스무 살.
Ages use native numbers + 살: 스무 살, 서른 살.
Ages are native numbers + 살. 스물 stays whole in 스물다섯.
Short form of 스물 used right before a counter: 스무 명, 스무 살.
스물 becomes 스무 right before a counter: 스무 살, but 스물한 살.
distractors: I've lived here for twenty years.

items.english: How old is your younger sibling?
distractors: How many siblings do you have?

items.note: Native tens: 열, 스물, 서른, 마흔, 쉰. Ages above that often switch to Sino-Korean.
distractors: My older brother has thirty books.

items.english: Excuse me, do you know what time it is?

items.note: Sino-Korean tens: 이십 (20), 삼십 (30), 오십 (50).
Clock hours are native (네 시), minutes Sino-Korean (오십오 분).

items.english: I have a meeting at 9 a.m.
items.note: 오전 = a.m., 오후 = p.m.; they come before the hour.
distractors: I have a meeting at 9 p.m.

good.english: Then you'll have to get up early.

items.note: 열 + 하나 = 열하나 (11); before a counter: 열한 시, 열두 개.
세 시 반 = half past three.

items.english: Class starts at half past eleven.
items.note: 열한 시 = 열 + 한 (from 하나); 반 adds half an hour.
distractors: Class ends at half past eleven.
Class starts at half past one.

items.english: I get up at eight in the morning.
distractors: I go to bed at eight in the evening.
I get up at seven in the morning.

items.english: I usually leave work at six.
distractors: I usually start work at six.
I usually leave work at seven.

items.note: 열두 시 = 열 + 두 (from 둘); 밤 열두 시 is midnight.
distractors: It closes at ten at night.

items.english: What time does the movie end?
distractors: What time does the movie start?

items.note: Minutes are Sino-Korean: 오 분, 십 분, 삼십 분.

items.english: How long does it take from home to the office?
distractors: How far is it from home to the office?
When do you leave for the office?
How do you get to the office?

bad.english: The office is on the third floor.

items.english: I worked out for an hour and a half.
items.note: Hours of duration use native numbers + 시간: 한 시간, 두 시간.
distractors: I worked out at half past one.
I worked out for half an hour.
I work out once a week.

items.english: How many cups of coffee do you drink a day?
distractors: How much is a cup of coffee?
What time do you drink coffee?

bad.english: I drink it at a café.

items.note: Native 번 counts times (두 번 = twice); Sino 번 names a number (이 번 = number two).

items.english: I work out three times a week.
items.note: 번 with native numbers counts times: 한 번, 두 번, 세 번.
distractors: I work out three days a month.
I work out for three hours a week.
I worked out three weeks ago.

good.english: What kind of exercise do you do?

items.english: I've been to Korea three times.
distractors: I've been in Korea for three years.
I'm coming to Korea for three weeks.

items.note: Sino-Korean + 번 names a number (십오 번 = no. 15); native + 번 counts times.
distractors: My seat is in row five.
My seat is by the window.

items.note: Floors use Sino-Korean numbers: 삼 층, 십오 층.

items.english: What floor is that restaurant on?
distractors: How many floors does the building have?

items.english: The restroom is on the third floor.
distractors: The restroom is on the first floor.
The restroom is next to the stairs.

items.note: Subway lines use Sino-Korean + 호선: 일 호선, 사 호선.
In phone numbers zero is 공; in maths and scores it is 영.
Phone numbers go digit by digit in Sino-Korean; zero is 공, the dash is read 에.

items.english: What day of the week is it tomorrow?
I work from Monday to Friday.
distractors: I work from Monday to Saturday.
I only work on Mondays and Fridays.
I'm off from Monday to Friday.

items.english: Are you free on Tuesday evening?
distractors: Are you free on Thursday evening?
What did you do on Tuesday evening?
Do you have dinner on Tuesdays?

good.english: Tuesday's a bit busy. How about Wednesday?

items.english: I have an exam on Thursday.
distractors: I had an exam on Thursday.
I have an exam on Tuesday.

good.english: Which mountain do you go to?

items.english: The meeting is on Wednesday at 2 p.m.
distractors: The meeting is on Wednesday at 2 a.m.
The meeting is on Tuesday at 2 p.m.
The meeting lasts two hours on Wednesday.

items.english: What did you do last Saturday?
distractors: What are you doing this Saturday?
Where did you go last Sunday?
What did you do last night?

good.english: I went to a friend's birthday party.

items.note: Months are Sino-Korean + 월: 일월, 이월, 삼월…
Asks for the day of the month: 며칠이에요? Never written 몇 일.

items.english: What's the date of your birthday?
items.note: Dates are Sino-Korean: 몇 월 며칠 asks for the month and the day.
distractors: What did you do on your birthday?
What day of the week is your birthday?

items.note: Six is 육, but June is 유월: the ㄱ drops.
June is 유월, not 육월; October is 시월, not 십월.
distractors: My birthday is on the sixteenth.

items.note: Ten is 십, but October is 시월: the ㅂ drops.

items.english: The weather in Korea is nice in October.
distractors: The weather in Korea is nice in June.
It rains a lot in Korea in October.

items.note: Month and day are both Sino-Korean: 삼월 일 일 = 3/1.

distractors: What day of the week is it today?

items.note: 천 alone is 1,000; say 천 원, not 일천 원.
Years are Sino-Korean + 년: 이천 년, 이천이십오 년.

items.english: I worked in Korea for three years.
distractors: I worked in Korea for three months.
I've been to Korea three times.
I'll work in Korea for three years.

items.note: Native count of months: 한 달, 두 달. Named months use 월.

items.korean: 한 달에 두 번 영화를 봐요.
items.english: I see a movie twice a month.
items.note: 달 counts months with native numbers (한 달, 두 달); 월 names them (이월).
distractors: I see a movie every two months.
I saw two movies this month.
I see a movie twice a week.
Do you have this bag in black?

items.note: Prices are Sino-Korean; 1,000 is just 천 and 100 just 백, never 일천 or 일백.
10,000 is 만 on its own: 만 원, never 일만 원.
distractors: I paid a hundred thousand won.

items.note: Big numbers group by 만: 팔만 오천 = 8 × 10,000 + 5,000.

good.english: Could you give me a discount?

items.english: Please take a thousand won off.
distractors: Please take ten thousand won off.
Please give me a thousand won.

items.note: Native numbers count the items (두 개), Sino-Korean gives the price (만 원).

items.english: A bottle of water is 1,000 won.
distractors: A bottle of water is 10,000 won.
A glass of water is 1,000 won.
Two bottles of water are 1,000 won.

items.note: 장 counts tickets, photos and sheets, with native numbers: 한 장, 두 장.

items.english: Could you take a photo of me?
items.note: 장 counts flat things: photos, tickets, sheets of paper.
distractors: Could you take a video of me?
Let me take a photo of you.

bad.english: It's a thousand won a sheet.

items.note: 대 counts cars, bikes, computers and phones: 차 두 대.

items.korean: 우리 집에 차가 두 대 있어요.
items.english: We have two cars at home.
items.note: 대 counts vehicles and machines: 차 한 대, 컴퓨터 두 대.
distractors: We have two bikes at home.
We have two rooms at home.
Our house is two stops away.
